newsitem.title: CANADA: Bank of Canada plans to close output gap-Freedman.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Canada plans to close output gap-Freedman.

text.p: Bank of Canada Deputy Governor Chuck Freedman said on Thursday the central bank's actions were aimed at closing the country's output gap, but added there was no set timetable to do so.
The central bank official also said economic growth would narrow the gap throughout 1997 and 1998. The Bank of Canada calculated the output gap was at 2.5 percent at the end of 1996.

"We have been trying to provide stimulus to the economy in order to close that gap," said Freedman. "We think those easier monetary conditions, lower interest rates in particular, are going to have a substantial effect on domestic demand."

Speaking to a Toronto business group, Freedman said the bank's goal of closing the gap between aggregate demand and potential output was linked to keeping the inflation rate within the Bank of Canada's 1.0-3.0 percent target range.

"We take action to bring about stimulative monetary conditions in order to try to close the gap in these circumstances because we think with that gap there still is that downward pressure on inflation that comes from the gap," said Freedman.

At the same time, Freedman said the central bank is cautious because it does not want aggregate demand surpassing capacity and creating inflation pressures. He said ideally the central bank would like to duplicate the U.S. experience, in which the economy is operating at full capacity without sparking inflation pressures.

"We think 1997 is going to be a good year for (Canadian) growth, it will take up slack," said Freedman. "We think 1998 will have considerable momentum as well and slack will be gradually taken up over that period."

Freedman made the comments on the output gap following a speech on the nature of the Bank of Canada's monetary conditions index. In the speech, Freedman noted that the Bank of Canada has no formal target range for the MCI and does not focus on it in a "mechanistic" fashion.
Instead, the MCI is one of a number of tools the bank uses to make judgements on on actions which affect monetary policy, he said.
